title: Salt in the water
word: reading the Isha in the original
hook: salt dissolved in water, and the Isha's riddle: that moves and moves not
carry: the one reality is far, near, and inside all this
tomorrow: can the order of words teach something all on its own?

segments.voice: Yesterday: the atman is worth more than the world, and atmahano, people who forget the self. Today the light comes back, in riddles, and the week comes back with it.

Sit on a train at a station, and when the train beside you starts to roll, there's a second where you honestly can't tell which one is moving. Still and moving at once, until you look out the other window. The Isha builds its next two verses on that second. Tad ejati tan naijati. That moves. That moves not. And it never names what that is. It just keeps pointing: tad, that, again and again, like something too big for a label.
screen: `WHICH TRAIN IS MOVING?` → `TAD EJATI: THAT MOVES.` → `TAN NAIJATI: THAT MOVES NOT.`

segments.voice: Verse four sets it up: anejad ekam manaso javiyo, unmoving, one, swifter than the mind. Verse five: tad ejati tan naijati. That moves, that moves not. Na, not, and ejati, moves, melt into naijati, one syllable holding a whole no. Then: tad dure, that is far; tad v antike, that is near. That is inside all this, and outside all this. To hear what that is, borrow a story from another Upanishad, the Chandogya. A father, Uddalaka, tells his son Shvetaketu to drop a lump of salt in water overnight. In the morning: bring me the salt. The boy can't find it. Sip from the top, says the father. Salty. The middle? Salty. The bottom? Salty. It's there all along, the father says; you just can't see it. That finest thing is the self of all this, and you are that: tat tvam asi. Here's the teaching. Brahman, the one reality, is beyond everything, faster than the mind, and also dissolved in every sip of the world, including you. Hindu schools read it differently: Advaita hears one reality and nothing else; Vishishtadvaita hears the Lord inside all he pervades. Now hold up the week: dharma kept at home, a despair that starts the path, the Lord in all this, offering before enjoying, action that doesn't bind, the self worth more than the world. And now the salt: that, everywhere.
screen: `MOVES AND NOT, FAR AND NEAR.` · `SALT IN THE WATER.` · `TAT TVAM ASI: YOU ARE THAT.` · `TWO SCHOOLS, AND THE WEEK.`

segments.voice: Keep the body still and listen for one sound that moves: traffic, wind, a fan, someone in the next room. Let it come close and go far while you stay where you are. Still, and the sound moving through: both true at once. If you pray, end with one quiet Om, the sound many Hindus use to point at that.
Reading the Isha in the original, verses four and five: that which moves and moves not, far and near, inside all this, like salt in the water.

fork.setup: a classmate reads 'that moves, that moves not' and says, 'so it's just confused.' what's the reader's answer?
options: the pairs are on purpose: each one stops a picture from settling.

fork.reveal: still and swifter than the mind, far and near, inside and outside: every pair stops a single picture, because Brahman is beyond them and in them, like salt in water.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: naijati, na plus ejati, moves not, with the not melted in.

trapdoor: what you thought: the verse is a paradox for its own sake.
what it means: that moves and moves not, far and near, inside and outside all this.
what a scholar hears: tat + na + ejati gives tan naijati by sandhi; javiyah is a comparative with manasah, 'than the mind.'

chat.says: dad keeps saying apply close to home. if i go far for college, am i far from all this?
options: the Isha says that is far and near, inside all this. like salt in water, it goes where you go.
yes; the Isha says the sacred is far off, so stay near home to keep it.
no; the Isha says it never moves, so it stays where you grew up.
chat.meaning: Tad dure tad v antike: that is far, that is near, inside and outside all this. Like Uddalaka's salt, Brahman is in every sip, wherever you are.

tie.story: Uddalaka showed his son that salt dissolved in water is in every sip though unseen, and the Isha says that is far and near at once.
tie.friend: Priya can go far for college without going far from what's sacred: it's inside all this, wherever she lives.
tie.you: where did you taste the salt this week?
